questiontext.text: In Input Space Partitioning (ISP), a characteristic divides the input domain into blocks. What is a block?

answer.text: A subset of the domain's values that the characteristic groups together and treats as one class

feedback.text: Correct — each block is one class of values produced by partitioning along that characteristic.

answer.text: A single concrete test case ready to run

feedback.text: A block is a class of values; a concrete test is one representative chosen from a block.

answer.text: A line of source code exercised by the input

feedback.text: ISP is black-box and describes the input domain, not code lines.

answer.text: The expected output the program should produce

feedback.text: That is an oracle result, not a block of the input domain.

generalfeedback.text: A characteristic partitions the input domain into blocks; each block is a set of values assumed to be handled equivalently, and one representative value is later chosen from each block.

questiontext.text: For one characteristic, its partition of the input domain is best described as which of the following?

answer.text: The collection of blocks that are pairwise disjoint and whose union is the whole domain

feedback.text: Correct — a partition is exactly a set of disjoint, complete blocks.

answer.text: Any collection of overlapping value ranges chosen for convenience

feedback.text: Overlap breaks disjointness, so overlapping ranges do not form a valid partition.

answer.text: The single most important value of the domain

feedback.text: A partition is a set of blocks covering the domain, not one value.

answer.text: The list of test cases produced by a coverage criterion

feedback.text: Tests come later; the partition is the division of the domain itself.

generalfeedback.text: A partition (for one characteristic) is a set of blocks that together are complete (cover the whole domain) and disjoint (no value in two blocks).

questiontext.text: The blocks of a characteristic are required to be disjoint. What does that mean?

answer.text: No value of the domain belongs to more than one block

feedback.text: Correct — disjoint means the blocks do not overlap.

answer.text: Every value of the domain belongs to some block

feedback.text: That describes completeness, not disjointness.

answer.text: All blocks contain the same number of values

feedback.text: Equal size is not required; disjointness only forbids overlap.

answer.text: There are exactly two blocks

feedback.text: Disjointness says nothing about how many blocks there are.

generalfeedback.text: Disjoint means the blocks are mutually exclusive: any given input value falls into at most one block of that characteristic.

questiontext.text: The blocks of a characteristic are required to be complete. What does that mean?

answer.text: The union of the blocks is the entire input domain — every value falls into some block

feedback.text: Correct — completeness means the blocks leave no value uncovered.

answer.text: No value belongs to two blocks

feedback.text: That describes disjointness, not completeness.

answer.text: Each block is tested with at least two values

feedback.text: Completeness is about covering the domain, not about how many values per block.

answer.text: The characteristic has at least three blocks

feedback.text: Completeness places no minimum on the number of blocks.

generalfeedback.text: Complete means the blocks cover the whole domain: taken together they contain every possible input value, so nothing is left unclassifiable.

questiontext.text: Once the blocks are defined, how does ISP turn them into concrete tests?

answer.text: Choose one representative value from each block used in a test

feedback.text: Correct — one representative per block stands in for the whole block.

answer.text: Use every value in every block exhaustively

feedback.text: Exhaustive enumeration is exactly what partitioning avoids.

answer.text: Pick values only from the largest block

feedback.text: Every block used in a test needs a representative, not just the largest one.

answer.text: Generate values randomly, ignoring the blocks

feedback.text: Then the blocks would play no role; ISP deliberately picks a representative per block.

generalfeedback.text: ISP relies on the assumption that a block's values are handled equivalently, so a single representative value per block is chosen to build each test.

questiontext.text: What are interface-based characteristics derived from?

answer.text: The parameters of the method under test, considered individually from its signature

feedback.text: Correct — interface-based characteristics come straight from the input parameters.

answer.text: The program's specification and intended behavior

feedback.text: That describes functionality-based characteristics.

answer.text: The internal control-flow graph of the code

feedback.text: ISP is black-box; interface-based characteristics use the parameters, not the CFG.

answer.text: The measured runtime of each test

feedback.text: Timing is unrelated to how characteristics are derived.

generalfeedback.text: Interface-based characteristics are read off the method's parameters one at a time (e.g. "is parameter x null?"). They are easy to derive but can miss relationships between parameters.

questiontext.text: What are functionality-based characteristics derived from?

answer.text: The specified behavior or semantics of the function, possibly combining several parameters

feedback.text: Correct — functionality-based characteristics come from what the function is supposed to do.

answer.text: Each parameter taken in isolation from the signature

feedback.text: That is the interface-based approach.

answer.text: The number of statements in the implementation

feedback.text: Statement counts are code metrics, not functionality-based characteristics.

answer.text: The compiler's optimization level

feedback.text: Compilation settings have nothing to do with deriving characteristics.

generalfeedback.text: Functionality-based characteristics come from the specification (e.g. "list is already sorted"), and may relate several parameters at once. They often yield better tests but require more domain understanding.

questiontext.text: What does Each Choice Coverage (ECC) require of a test set?

answer.text: Every block of every characteristic must appear in at least one test

feedback.text: Correct — that is exactly the each-choice requirement.

answer.text: Every combination of blocks across all characteristics must appear

feedback.text: That is All Combinations Coverage, which is far stronger.

answer.text: Every pair of blocks from every pair of characteristics must appear together

feedback.text: That is Pair-Wise Coverage, not Each Choice.

answer.text: Exactly one test is needed regardless of the blocks

feedback.text: One test cannot include two different blocks of the same characteristic.

generalfeedback.text: ECC only asks that each block of each characteristic be used at least once somewhere in the test set — the weakest of the standard ISP criteria.

questiontext.text: What does All Combinations Coverage (ACoC) require of a test set?

answer.text: Every combination of one block from each characteristic must appear in some test

feedback.text: Correct — ACoC covers the full cross-product of blocks.

answer.text: Only that each block appears at least once

feedback.text: That is Each Choice Coverage, which is weaker.

answer.text: Only that every pair of blocks appears together

feedback.text: That is Pair-Wise Coverage, weaker than ACoC.

answer.text: That a single base test is varied one characteristic at a time

feedback.text: That describes Base Choice Coverage, not ACoC.

generalfeedback.text: ACoC requires every combination of blocks — one from each characteristic — so the number of tests is the product of the block counts.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has two characteristics with 2 and 3 blocks. How many tests does All Combinations Coverage (ACoC) require?

feedback.text: Correct — 2 × 3 = 6, the product of the block counts.
5 is the sum 2 + 3; ACoC multiplies the block counts.
3 is the larger block count (that is Each Choice), not All Combinations.
9 does not match 2 × 3.

generalfeedback.text: ACoC is the product of the block counts: 2 × 3 = 6.

name.text: ACoC count for three binary characteristics

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics, each with 2 blocks. How many tests does ACoC require?

feedback.text: Correct — 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
6 is the sum 2 + 2 + 2; ACoC multiplies.
2 is one block count (Each Choice), not All Combinations.
4 ignores one characteristic; the product over all three is 8.

generalfeedback.text: ACoC is the product of the block counts: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

name.text: ECC count equals the largest block count

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics with 2, 5, and 3 blocks. What is the minimum number of tests for Each Choice Coverage (ECC)?

feedback.text: Correct — ECC needs at least the largest block count, max(2,5,3) = 5.
10 is the sum of the block counts; blocks can be reused across characteristics within one test.
30 is the product (All Combinations), far more than ECC needs.
3 is not enough to cover the characteristic with 5 blocks.

generalfeedback.text: Each test picks one block per characteristic, so covering every block needs at least as many tests as the largest block count: max(2,5,3) = 5.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has two characteristics with 4 and 2 blocks. What is the minimum number of tests for Each Choice Coverage (ECC)?

feedback.text: Correct — ECC needs at least max(4,2) = 4 tests.
8 is the product (All Combinations), not the each-choice minimum.
6 is the sum of the block counts; ECC reuses blocks within a test.
2 cannot cover the characteristic that has 4 blocks.

generalfeedback.text: ECC equals the largest block count: max(4,2) = 4. The 2-block characteristic's blocks are simply reused within those four tests.

name.text: A valid characteristic and its blocks

questiontext.text: For an integer input x, which of these is a well-formed ISP characteristic with disjoint, complete blocks?

answer.text: "Sign of x" with blocks {x < 0}, {x = 0}, {x > 0}

feedback.text: Correct — these three blocks are disjoint and cover every integer.

answer.text: "Size of x" with blocks {x < 10}, {x > 5}

feedback.text: Values 6..9 fall in both blocks, so they overlap (not disjoint).

answer.text: "Range of x" with blocks {x < 0}, {x > 0}

feedback.text: The value 0 belongs to no block, so this is incomplete.

answer.text: "Value of x" with one block {x = 7}

feedback.text: Every other integer is uncovered, so this partition is incomplete.

generalfeedback.text: A well-formed characteristic partitions the domain into disjoint, complete blocks. "Sign of x" as negative / zero / positive does exactly that for the integers.

questiontext.text: Input Space Partitioning is a black-box technique: it models the input domain and does not require access to the source code.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — ISP derives characteristics from parameters and the specification, not from code.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: ISP works on the input domain (interface- or functionality-based), so it needs no source code.

generalfeedback.text: ISP is a black-box, input-domain technique. Characteristics come from the method's parameters (interface-based) or its specified behavior (functionality-based), so the implementation is not needed.

questiontext.text: A characteristic "string length L" is split into blocks {L < 10}, {10 ≤ L ≤ 20}, {L > 15}. Is this a valid partition, and why?

answer.text: Invalid — the blocks are not disjoint (e.g. L = 18 falls in both {10 ≤ L ≤ 20} and {L > 15})

feedback.text: Correct — 16..20 lie in two blocks at once, breaking disjointness.

answer.text: Valid — the blocks are disjoint and complete

feedback.text: They are not disjoint: values 16..20 belong to two blocks.

answer.text: Invalid — some lengths are left uncovered (incomplete)

feedback.text: Every length is covered; the defect here is overlap, not a gap.

answer.text: Valid — overlap between blocks is allowed in ISP

feedback.text: Overlap is not allowed; blocks of a partition must be disjoint.

generalfeedback.text: Lengths 16..20 satisfy both {10 ≤ L ≤ 20} and {L > 15}, so the blocks overlap. A valid partition must be disjoint, so this is invalid.

name.text: Spot the gap in a partition

questiontext.text: A characteristic "age" (non-negative integer) is split into blocks {0..17}, {19..65}, {> 65}. Is this a valid partition, and why?

answer.text: Invalid — it is incomplete: age 18 belongs to no block

feedback.text: Correct — 18 is missing, so the blocks do not cover the whole domain.

answer.text: Valid — the blocks are disjoint and complete

feedback.text: Age 18 is uncovered, so completeness fails.

answer.text: Invalid — the blocks overlap at 65

feedback.text: 65 is only in {19..65}; there is no overlap. The defect is the missing 18.

answer.text: Valid — small gaps are acceptable in ISP

feedback.text: Gaps violate completeness; every domain value must fall into some block.

generalfeedback.text: Age 18 is not in {0..17}, {19..65}, or {> 65}, so the partition is incomplete and therefore invalid.

questiontext.text: A characteristic "temperature T (integer °C)" is split into blocks {T < 0}, {0 ≤ T ≤ 100}, {T > 100}. Is this a valid partition?

answer.text: Valid — the three blocks are disjoint and together cover every integer temperature

feedback.text: Correct — no overlap and no gap, so it is a proper partition.

answer.text: Invalid — the blocks overlap at 0 and 100

feedback.text: 0 is only in the middle block and 100 only in the middle block; there is no overlap.

answer.text: Invalid — temperatures below 0 are uncovered

feedback.text: {T < 0} covers them, so nothing is uncovered.

answer.text: Invalid — a partition may have at most two blocks

feedback.text: A characteristic may have any number of blocks; three is fine.

generalfeedback.text: The blocks {T < 0}, {0..100}, {T > 100} are mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive over the integers, so the partition is disjoint and complete — valid.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics with 4, 3, and 2 blocks. How many tests does All Combinations Coverage (ACoC) require?

feedback.text: Correct — 4 × 3 × 2 = 24.
9 is the sum 4 + 3 + 2; ACoC multiplies the block counts.
12 is the product of only the two largest (a PWC lower bound), not all three.
4 is the largest single block count (Each Choice), not All Combinations.

generalfeedback.text: ACoC = product of the block counts = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has four characteristics with 3, 3, 5, and 2 blocks. What is the minimum number of tests for Each Choice Coverage (ECC)?

feedback.text: Correct — ECC needs at least max(3,3,5,2) = 5 tests.
13 is the sum of the block counts; ECC reuses blocks within each test.
90 is the product (All Combinations), not the each-choice minimum.
4 is not enough to cover the characteristic that has 5 blocks.

generalfeedback.text: ECC equals the largest block count: max(3,3,5,2) = 5.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics with 2, 4, and 3 blocks. How many tests does Base Choice Coverage (BCC) require?

feedback.text: 9 is the sum of the block counts; BCC is 1 + Σ(blocks - 1).
24 is the product (All Combinations), not the base-choice count.
6 forgets the +1 base test: 1 + (1 + 3 + 2) = 7.

generalfeedback.text: BCC = 1 + Σ(b_i - 1) = 1 + (1 + 3 + 2) = 7: one base test plus varying each characteristic through its non-base blocks.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics with 2, 2, and 4 blocks. How many tests does Base Choice Coverage (BCC) require?

feedback.text: 8 is the sum of the block counts; BCC is 1 + Σ(blocks - 1).
16 is the product (All Combinations), not the base-choice count.
5 forgets the +1 base test: 1 + (1 + 1 + 3) = 6.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics with 4, 3, and 2 blocks. What is the minimum number of tests any Pair-Wise Coverage (PWC) set must contain?

feedback.text: Correct — at least the product of the two largest block counts, 4 × 3 = 12.
24 is the full All Combinations product; PWC needs fewer.
9 is the sum of the block counts, unrelated to the pairwise lower bound.
4 (the largest single block count) is the Each Choice minimum, not the pairwise bound.

generalfeedback.text: Covering every pair from the two largest characteristics (4 and 3 blocks) already needs all 4 × 3 = 12 of their combinations, so any PWC set has at least 12 tests.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has four characteristics with 2, 5, 3, and 2 blocks. What is the minimum number of tests any Pair-Wise Coverage (PWC) set must contain?

feedback.text: Correct — the product of the two largest block counts, 5 × 3 = 15.
60 is the full All Combinations product; PWC needs fewer.
12 is the sum of the block counts, not the pairwise lower bound.
5 (the largest single block count) is the Each Choice minimum, not the pairwise bound.

generalfeedback.text: The PWC lower bound is the product of the two largest block counts: 5 × 3 = 15.

questiontext.text: For int indexOf(List list, Object target), a tester defines the characteristic "is list null?" with blocks {null}, {non-null}. How is this characteristic best classified?

answer.text: Interface-based — it comes directly from a single parameter of the signature

feedback.text: Correct — nullness of one parameter is read straight off the interface.

answer.text: Functionality-based — it comes from the specified search behavior

feedback.text: It is derived from the parameter itself, not from what indexOf is specified to do.

answer.text: Neither — nullness cannot be a characteristic

feedback.text: Nullness of a reference parameter is a common, valid interface-based characteristic.

answer.text: It depends on the implementation's control flow

feedback.text: ISP is black-box; this characteristic is defined without looking at code.

generalfeedback.text: "Is list null?" is derived from one parameter considered on its own, which is the defining trait of an interface-based characteristic.

questiontext.text: For a sorting routine sort(int[] a), a tester defines the characteristic "is a already sorted ascending?" with blocks {already sorted}, {not sorted}. How is this best classified?

answer.text: Functionality-based — it comes from the meaning of sorting, not from the parameter's type alone

feedback.text: Correct — "already sorted" is a property of the specified behavior over the input's contents.

answer.text: Interface-based — it comes directly from the array parameter's type

feedback.text: The type is just "int[]"; being already-sorted is a semantic property, not read off the signature.

answer.text: It is not a valid characteristic because it depends on values

feedback.text: Depending on the input's contents is exactly what functionality-based characteristics do.

answer.text: It is a structural (white-box) characteristic

feedback.text: ISP is black-box; this comes from the specification of sorting, not the code structure.

generalfeedback.text: "Already sorted?" reflects the semantics of the sorting task and the array's contents, so it is functionality-based rather than interface-based.

questiontext.text: A characteristic "score S" has blocks {S ≤ 50}, {40 ≤ S ≤ 90}, {S > 90}. Which value demonstrates that the partition is not disjoint?

feedback.text: Correct — 45 is in both {S ≤ 50} and {40 ≤ S ≤ 90}, proving overlap.
20 is only in {S ≤ 50}; it does not show overlap.
95 is only in {S > 90}; it does not show overlap.
91 is only in {S > 90}; it does not show overlap.

generalfeedback.text: The blocks {S ≤ 50} and {40 ≤ S ≤ 90} both contain 40..50. Any value there, such as 45, lies in two blocks and proves the partition is not disjoint.

questiontext.text: A characteristic "quantity Q (integer)" has blocks {Q < 0}, {1 ≤ Q ≤ 100}, {Q > 100}. Which value demonstrates that the partition is incomplete?

feedback.text: Correct — 0 is not negative, not in 1..100, and not > 100, so it is uncovered.
50 is covered by {1 ≤ Q ≤ 100}.
-5 is covered by {Q < 0}.
200 is covered by {Q > 100}.

generalfeedback.text: Q = 0 falls into none of {Q < 0}, {1..100}, {Q > 100}, so the partition leaves a gap and is incomplete.

name.text: Extra tests ACoC needs over ECC

questiontext.text: An ISP model has two characteristics with 3 and 2 blocks. How many more tests does All Combinations Coverage require than the Each Choice minimum?

answer.text: 3 (ACoC = 6, ECC = 3)

feedback.text: Correct — 3 × 2 = 6 for ACoC and max(3,2) = 3 for ECC, a difference of 3.

answer.text: 0 (they are always equal)

feedback.text: ACoC = 6 but ECC = 3, so they differ here.

answer.text: 6 (ACoC = 6, ECC = 0)

feedback.text: ECC is not 0; it is max(3,2) = 3, so the difference is 3.

answer.text: 2 (ACoC = 5, ECC = 3)

feedback.text: ACoC is the product 3 × 2 = 6, not 5, so the difference is 3.

generalfeedback.text: ACoC = 3 × 2 = 6 and ECC = max(3,2) = 3, so ACoC needs 6 - 3 = 3 more tests.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics with 2, 3, and 2 blocks. How many tests does Base Choice Coverage (BCC) require?

feedback.text: 7 is the sum of the block counts; BCC is 1 + Σ(blocks - 1).
12 is the product (All Combinations), not the base-choice count.
4 forgets the +1 base test: 1 + (1 + 2 + 1) = 5.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has four characteristics with 4, 3, 3, and 2 blocks. How many tests does Base Choice Coverage (BCC) require?

feedback.text: 12 is the sum of the block counts; BCC is 1 + Σ(blocks - 1).
72 is the product (All Combinations), not the base-choice count.
8 forgets the +1 base test: 1 + (3 + 2 + 2 + 1) = 9.

name.text: Pick the BCC test set from a base

questiontext.text: Characteristics A, B, C have blocks A∈{a1,a2}, B∈{b1,b2,b3}, C∈{c1,c2}. The base choice is (a1, b1, c1). Which set of tests is exactly the Base Choice Coverage set?

feedback.text: Correct — the base test plus one test per non-base block, changing exactly one characteristic each time.

answer.text: (a1,b1,c1), (a2,b2,c2) — two tests

feedback.text: This changes several characteristics at once and misses most non-base blocks; it is not the BCC set.

answer.text: All 12 combinations of A × B × C

feedback.text: That is All Combinations Coverage, not Base Choice.

answer.text: (a2,b2,c2), (a2,b3,c2) — varying from a non-base test

feedback.text: BCC varies from the designated base test (a1,b1,c1), holding the others at their base values.

generalfeedback.text: BCC keeps the base (a1,b1,c1) and changes one characteristic at a time to each non-base block: a2; b2; b3; c2. That yields 1 + (1 + 2 + 1) = 5 tests.

questiontext.text: Which subsumption chain correctly orders these ISP criteria (each subsumes the next)?

answer.text: ACoC ⊇ PWC ⊇ ECC

feedback.text: Correct — all combinations subsume pairwise, which subsumes each choice.

answer.text: ECC ⊇ PWC ⊇ ACoC

feedback.text: This reverses the order; ECC is the weakest, so it cannot subsume the others.

answer.text: PWC ⊇ ACoC ⊇ ECC

feedback.text: ACoC subsumes PWC, not the other way around.

answer.text: ACoC ⊇ ECC ⊇ PWC

feedback.text: ECC does not subsume PWC; PWC is the stronger of the two.

generalfeedback.text: All Combinations covers every pair, so ACoC subsumes PWC; Pair-Wise covers each single block, so PWC subsumes ECC. Hence ACoC ⊇ PWC ⊇ ECC.

questiontext.text: Suppose a characteristic's blocks overlap, so some value v belongs to two blocks. Why does this make the partition invalid for ISP?

answer.text: A value that maps to two blocks makes block membership ambiguous, so coverage of "each block" is ill-defined and a chosen value may unintentionally satisfy two blocks at once

feedback.text: Correct — disjointness is what makes "the block of a value" well-defined.

answer.text: Overlap makes the model too small to test

feedback.text: Overlap does not shrink the model; it makes membership ambiguous.

answer.text: Overlap forces the use of All Combinations Coverage

feedback.text: Overlap does not dictate a coverage criterion; it violates the partition definition.

answer.text: Overlap is fine as long as the blocks are complete

feedback.text: Completeness does not repair a disjointness violation; both are required.

generalfeedback.text: If v is in two blocks, then "cover each block" and "the representative of a value's block" become ambiguous — one test value may count for two blocks, undermining the criterion. Disjointness removes that ambiguity.

questiontext.text: Suppose a characteristic's blocks miss some domain value w (no block contains it). Why is this partition invalid for ISP?

answer.text: An input equal to w cannot be classified into any block, so a legitimate part of the domain would never be scheduled for testing

feedback.text: Correct — completeness guarantees every input is represented by some block.

answer.text: The number of tests would become infinite

feedback.text: A gap does not change the test count; it leaves part of the domain unmodeled.

answer.text: Each Choice Coverage would then be impossible to satisfy

feedback.text: ECC could still be satisfied on the defined blocks; the problem is the unmodeled value w.

answer.text: Incompleteness is acceptable if the blocks are disjoint

feedback.text: Disjointness does not repair a coverage gap; both properties are required.

generalfeedback.text: A partition must be complete so that every possible input belongs to exactly one block. If w belongs to no block, that input is unmodeled and would be systematically left out of the test design.

name.text: Choosing a criterion under a test budget

questiontext.text: A model has 5 characteristics, each with 4 blocks. All Combinations needs 4^5 = 1024 tests, which the budget cannot afford, but you still want each block exercised together with a common base configuration. Which criterion best fits a budget of roughly 16 tests?

answer.text: Base Choice Coverage — 1 + 5 × (4-1) = 16 tests, varying each block from a base

feedback.text: Correct — BCC hits exactly 16 here and exercises every block relative to a base configuration.

answer.text: All Combinations Coverage — 1024 tests

feedback.text: 1024 is far over the budget; that is the criterion being ruled out.

answer.text: Pair-Wise Coverage — at least 4 × 4 = 16 but typically more

feedback.text: PWC's lower bound is 16, but a real pairwise set for five 4-block characteristics needs more than 16 and does not use a single base configuration.

answer.text: Each Choice Coverage — 4 tests

feedback.text: ECC needs only 4 tests but does not exercise blocks against a common base as asked.

generalfeedback.text: BCC = 1 + Σ(b_i - 1) = 1 + 5 × 3 = 16, right at the budget, and by construction it varies each block one at a time from a base test — matching the stated goal.

name.text: MBCC count with two base tests

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics with 3, 2, and 2 blocks. Using Multiple Base Choice Coverage with 2 base tests (one base choice per characteristic in each), how many tests result? Vary one characteristic at a time from each base test.

feedback.text: Correct — each base contributes 1 + (2 + 1 + 1) = 5 tests, and 2 × 5 = 10.
5 is the single-base (BCC) count; MBCC with 2 bases doubles it to 10.
12 is the ACoC product (3 × 2 × 2) doubled would be 24; MBCC here is 2 × 5 = 10.
7 is not consistent with m × (1 + Σ(b_i - 1)); the correct value is 2 × 5 = 10.

generalfeedback.text: With m base tests and one base choice per characteristic, MBCC = m × (1 + Σ(b_i - 1)). Here BCC = 1 + (2 + 1 + 1) = 5, so MBCC = 2 × 5 = 10.

questiontext.text: What is the subsumption relationship between Multiple Base Choice Coverage (MBCC) and Base Choice Coverage (BCC)?

answer.text: MBCC subsumes BCC — using several base tests includes the coverage of a single base test

feedback.text: Correct — MBCC ⊇ BCC ⊇ ECC.

answer.text: BCC subsumes MBCC

feedback.text: This reverses the direction; more base tests can only add coverage.

answer.text: They are incomparable — neither subsumes the other

feedback.text: MBCC is a generalization of BCC and always covers what BCC does.

answer.text: They are identical criteria

feedback.text: MBCC uses multiple base tests, so it can require strictly more tests than BCC.

generalfeedback.text: MBCC generalizes BCC by using more than one base test, so every BCC requirement is met by MBCC: MBCC ⊇ BCC ⊇ ECC.

name.text: ACoC count for four binary characteristics

questiontext.text: An ISP model has four characteristics, each with 2 blocks. How many tests does All Combinations Coverage require?

feedback.text: 8 is 2^3; there are four characteristics, so the product is 2^4 = 16.
4 is the number of pairs of blocks summed; ACoC multiplies all four block counts.
9 = 1 + 4 × 2 is a base-choice-style count, not the ACoC product.

generalfeedback.text: ACoC = 2^4 = 16, the product of the four block counts.

name.text: PWC lower bound with tied largest counts

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics with 4, 4, and 2 blocks. What is the minimum number of tests any Pair-Wise Coverage set must contain?

feedback.text: Correct — the two largest block counts are 4 and 4, so the lower bound is 4 × 4 = 16.
32 is the full All Combinations product (4 × 4 × 2); PWC needs fewer.
10 is the sum of the block counts, not the pairwise lower bound.
8 (4 × 2) uses the wrong pair; the two largest are both 4, giving 16.

generalfeedback.text: The PWC lower bound is the product of the two largest block counts. Both largest are 4, so the bound is 4 × 4 = 16. (Actual pairwise sets may need a few more tests, but never fewer.)

name.text: PWC equals ACoC for two characteristics

questiontext.text: When a model has exactly two characteristics, Pair-Wise Coverage and All Combinations Coverage require the same number of tests.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — with only one pair of characteristics, covering every pair of blocks is the full cross-product.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: With two characteristics the single pair's block combinations are exactly the All Combinations set, so PWC = ACoC here.

generalfeedback.text: PWC requires every pair of blocks from every pair of characteristics. With just two characteristics there is only one pair, and covering all of its block pairs is precisely b1 × b2 — the same as ACoC.

questiontext.text: Which statement about Pair-Wise Coverage (PWC) and Base Choice Coverage (BCC) is correct?

answer.text: Neither subsumes the other — PWC and BCC are incomparable

feedback.text: Correct — PWC guarantees pairs but not base-variation; BCC guarantees base-variation but not all pairs.

answer.text: PWC subsumes BCC

feedback.text: A pairwise set need not include a single base test varied one characteristic at a time, so it does not always satisfy BCC.

answer.text: BCC subsumes PWC

feedback.text: A base-choice set covers only Σ(b_i - 1) + 1 tests and misses most block pairs, so it does not satisfy PWC.

answer.text: They are equivalent criteria

feedback.text: They impose different requirements and generally produce different test sets.

generalfeedback.text: PWC and BCC are incomparable: both subsume ECC, but PWC covers all block pairs (not base variations) while BCC covers base variations (not all pairs).

questiontext.text: A characteristic "discount tier by amount A" is defined as {A < 100}, {100 ≤ A ≤ 500}, {A ≥ 500}. It is invalid. What is the minimal fix that makes it a valid partition?

answer.text: Change one bound so 500 is in exactly one block, e.g. {A < 100}, {100 ≤ A < 500}, {A ≥ 500}

feedback.text: Correct — the only defect is that 500 sits in two blocks; excluding it from one restores disjointness while keeping completeness.

answer.text: Delete the middle block entirely

feedback.text: That would leave 100..499 uncovered, creating an incompleteness gap.

answer.text: Add a fourth block {A = 500}

feedback.text: 500 would still remain in the existing blocks too, so the overlap is not removed.

answer.text: Nothing — the partition is already valid

feedback.text: 500 satisfies both {100 ≤ A ≤ 500} and {A ≥ 500}, so it is not disjoint.

generalfeedback.text: The value 500 lies in both the middle block and {A ≥ 500}, breaking disjointness. Making the middle block {100 ≤ A < 500} removes the overlap while still covering every amount, yielding a valid partition.

name.text: Does the base choice change the BCC count?

questiontext.text: Two testers model the same characteristics with 3, 2, and 2 blocks but pick different base choices. How do their Base Choice Coverage test sets compare?

answer.text: Both sets have the same size, 1 + (2 + 1 + 1) = 5, though the concrete test values differ

feedback.text: Correct — the BCC count 1 + Σ(b_i - 1) is independent of which block is chosen as the base.

answer.text: The set built from the "larger" base is always bigger

feedback.text: Block counts, not the chosen base, fix the size; both are 1 + Σ(b_i - 1) = 5.

answer.text: One set will satisfy ACoC and the other will not

feedback.text: Neither BCC set reaches ACoC (which needs 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 tests); base choice does not change that.

answer.text: The sizes differ by the number of characteristics

feedback.text: Both sizes equal 1 + Σ(b_i - 1) = 5 regardless of the base; the base only changes which values appear.

generalfeedback.text: BCC always produces 1 + Σ(b_i - 1) tests = 1 + (2 + 1 + 1) = 5 here. Changing the base choice changes which concrete tests are generated but not the count or the criterion satisfied.

name.text: MBCC count with three base tests

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics, each with 2 blocks. Using Multiple Base Choice Coverage with 3 base tests (one base choice per characteristic in each), varying one characteristic at a time from each base, how many tests result?

feedback.text: Correct — each base contributes 1 + (1 + 1 + 1) = 4 tests, and 3 × 4 = 12.
4 is the single-base (BCC) count; with 3 bases it becomes 3 × 4 = 12.
8 is the ACoC product (2 × 2 × 2); MBCC here is 3 × 4 = 12.
7 does not match m × (1 + Σ(b_i - 1)); the correct value is 3 × 4 = 12.

generalfeedback.text: MBCC = m × (1 + Σ(b_i - 1)). Here BCC = 1 + (1 + 1 + 1) = 4, so with 3 base tests MBCC = 3 × 4 = 12.
